title: Latency Is a Budget. Humanlike Is the Goal. — Jesse Hall, LiveKit
talk_summary: LiveKit argues real-time voice agents should be judged by human-like end-to-end conversation within a latency budget, not component leaderboards. It recommends measuring perceived latency, making long tool calls async, and evaluating the whole stack against outcome-based simulated scenarios.

takeaways.what_they_do: They run a complete working agent against hundreds of simulated real tasks, swap model stacks with identical inputs, and score end outcomes rather than component benchmarks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: test the conversation, not the components
takeaways.numbers: hundreds of simulated callers; 88% voice evals; 380 ms first speech

takeaways.technique: Route by task-level eval, not leaderboard
takeaways.what_they_do: They compare whole agent stacks on identical scenarios and pick the stack that meets the outcome bar inside the latency budget, instead of picking models from generic leaderboards.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Every model sees the exact identical input byte for byte.

takeaways.what_they_do: A tool returns an initial update immediately and keeps working in the background, so the agent can continue instead of blocking on a long operation.
takeaways.numbers: tools can take 2, 10, 40+ seconds; anything over a second should go async

takeaways.what_they_do: They score whether the right real-world outcome happened and penalize things completion scores miss, such as unnecessary questions, extra steps, invented tool calls, or leaked data.
They set a fixed end-to-end latency budget and measure what the user actually experiences, not provider dashboard metrics like time to first byte.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Measure perceived latency. Spend whatever budget is left on model quality, not on speed that doesn't matter.
takeaways.numbers: 1.5 s end-to-end still holds; closer to 600 ms feels human
